notes.text: They journeyed according to the commandment of the Lord, led by the pillar of cloud and fire, and yet they came to a place where there was no water for them to drink — We may be in the way of our duty, and yet meet with troubles, which Providence brings us into for the trial of our faith.

glossa.text:
*All the multitude of the children of Israel therefore setting forward,* etc. ((ORIG., hom. 11 in Exod.)) All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, and are assailed by enemies: and he who walks the road of this life ought always to be ready and to stand in the camp. Whence all the synagogue of the children of Israel set forward from the desert of Sin according to their camps by the word of God. There is indeed one Synagogue of the Lord. but it is divided into four camps, which are described in the book of Numbers as placed round about the tabernacle of the Lord. Do thou therefore, armed and serving in the camp of the Lord, not entangle thyself in secular business, and keep watch always in the camp of the Lord, that it may be said of thee that thou hast set forward by the word of the Lord from the desert of Sin, and comest into Raphidim. Now Sin is interpreted *temptation*; Raphidim, *soundness of judgment:* he who comes well out of temptation comes to soundness of judgment. For in the day of judgment he will be sound. Whence Apocalypse II: *To him that overcometh, I will give of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.* He therefore comes to soundness of judgment who orders his words well in judgment.

*Sin.* Here Sin is taken specially for one station out of those five which were from the Red Sea as far as mount Sina, which Josephus describes by name. For in general that whole desert is called Sin, as also Raphidim is.

*They encamped in Raphidim. ((HIERON. de Loc. Hebr., tom. III.))* It is a place in the desert beside mount Horeb. And it is to be known that the whole wilderness as far as mount Sinai is called Sin, and that from the whole province the place of a single station also took its name, as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province. In this solitude there are five stations, Zuph, and the desert of Sin, Alus, Depheca, Raphidim. Whence it is well said that *all the multitude of the children of Israel set forward from the desert of Sin by their stations according to the word of the Lord, and they came into Raphidim.* Whence it is plain that many stations are denoted by the name of one region.

*The people therefore thirsted there,* etc. ((ORIG., ubi supra )). Another reading: *The people,* he says, *thirsted for water, and murmured against Moses.* It was enough to say that *he thirsted,* what need was there to add *water?* The addition is not superfluous. There are therefore diverse thirsts, and each man has his own. They who are good hunger and thirst after justice ((Matth. V)). Others too say: *My soul hath thirsted after thee, O God ((Psal. XLI))* . But they who are sinners suffer not the thirst of water, not the hunger of bread, but of hearing the word of God. The people therefore thirsted for water, which ought to have thirsted for justice. But God, the instructor of the simple, the master of the unwise, corrects faults and amends errors, saying to Moses that he take the rod, and strike the rock, and bring forth waters. For he wills them now to drink of the rock and to make progress, and to come to the inner mysteries. For they murmured against Moses, and therefore the Lord commands that he show them the rock whereof they may drink. For if there is anyone who, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the law according to the letter displeases him, because in many things it seems not to hold together, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, that from it he may drink and repair his thirst. But this rock does not give waters unless it is struck, and when struck it brings forth fountains: for Christ, being struck and slain upon the cross, brought forth the fountains of the New Testament. Whence Zacharias VIII: *I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.* For unless he had been struck, and blood and water had gone forth from his side, we should all suffer thirst for the word of God. Whence: *And they drank of the spiritual rock that followed them: and the rock was Christ ((I Cor. X))*.

((ISID.)) The people, thirsting for water, murmured against Moses: therefore God commands that he show them the rock whereof they may drink. But if anyone, reading Moses, murmurs against him, and the letter of the law displeases him, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, that from it he may drink and repair his thirst.

*Go before the people,* etc. Not Moses alone leads the people to the waters, but also the elders of the people. For not the law alone announces Christ, but also the prophets and the patriarchs and all the elders by birth.

*And the rod,* etc. ((AUG., quaest. 64 in Exod.)) It is read that Aaron, not Moses, struck the river with the rod. For Moses divided the sea with that same rod, not the river. What then does this mean: *Take the rod wherewith thou didst strike the river?* Or did he perhaps call the sea a river? and is an example of this manner of speech to be sought? Or was what Aaron did rather attributed to Moses, because through Moses God commanded the things which Aaron did, and in the one was the authority, in the other the ministry? Whence: *He shall be to thee for the people, but thou to him in those things which are unto God.*
*And thou shalt strike the rock.* Christ, who was struck upon the cross by the Jews: to whom the rod came near, that is, the wood of the passion, that water might remain for the faithful.

notes.text: God's — Above all that are called God's angels, earthly potentates, and especially the false gods of the Heathen.
Hand — Under his government. Strength - The strongest or highest mountains.
Pasture — Whom he feeds and keeps in his own pasture, or in the land which he hath appropriated to himself. The sheep - Which are under his special care. Today - Forthwith or presently.
Harden not — By obstinate unbelief. Provocation - In that bold and wicked contest with God in the wilderness. Temptation - In the day in which you tempted me.
Works — Both of mercy, and of justice.

Do err — Their hearts are insincere and bent to backsliding. Not known - After all my teaching and discoveries of myself to them; they did not know, nor consider, those great things which I had wrought for them.

My rest — Into the promised land, which is called the rest, Deut. xii, 9. This psalm is a part of that which was delivered to Asaph and his brethren, 1 Chron. xvi, 7, on occasion of bringing up the ark to the city of David. Here is a call to praise God, as a great and glorious God, ver. 1-9. To rejoice in his judging all the world, ver. 10-13.

glossa.text: *Come, let us rejoice.* ((THEOD.)) King Josias was exceedingly pious, etc., *as far as* but the psalm is framed in the person of Josias, and of the priests of God. ((CASS.)) Concerning the time of grace, in which there is an entering into rest, the prophet, describing the praises of God, first invites the Jews, whom he foresaw to be able to resist Christ.

*His face,* etc. ((AUG., CASS.)) The sight of the judge to come, lest there be anything then in us to be sifted. *In confession.* ((AUG.)) Praising him, accusing ourselves, etc., *as far as* of which praise the psalm treats. *In psalms let us make a joyful noise.* *psalmi*; read *psalmis*, "in psalms" What we say in psalms, or do, let us feel in jubilation.
*Above all gods.* Or rather he calls men gods, over whom he is king, not over demons.
*For in his hand,* etc. ((CASS.)) After the greatness of the Lord foretold, he comes to his clemency.

*The sea.* ((AUG.)) The world, whose waves God confines within a bound, not suffering us to be tempted above that which we are able ((I Cor. X)); which waves also make increase for us, God working it, nor do the scandals hurt thee, which receive their measure from God.

*Come, let us adore.* ((CASS.)) First he called the untaught to exultation: now, the glory of God being shown, he calls to penance, which is the harder. *Let us weep.* ((AUG.)) If perchance you are solicitous concerning the sins which have made you far off, weep: a tear extinguishes the flame of sin which burns in the conscience. *Who made us.* Behold great confidence: for of thyself thou canst fail, thyself thou canst not remake, he remakes thee who made thee.

*And we are the people,* etc. ((AUG.)) Elegantly is the order of the words changed: He did not say the sheep of the pasture and the people of his hand, that thou mayest understand those very ones to be sheep who are the people, sheep of his hand, not those which from afar, because they are, and sheep which we did not make, but he himself by his own grace made us sheep.

*To-day if you shall hear the voice,* etc. ((CASS.)) But we are the people and the sheep. But to all these a condition is set forth, *if you shall hear his voice,* which voice he subjoins, *To-day. Harden not.* ((ID.)) Now Christ himself admonishes, lest they be hardened, lest it befall them as it did the fathers.
*As in the provocation.* ((ID.)) The majesty of Christ speaking, etc., *as far as* the fault of the parents is recalled, that the vengeance may be feared.
*Forty years.* ((AUG.)) By forty years he signifies all the ages, etc., *as far as* as he himself says: *I am with you unto the consummation of the world.*

notes.text: Being justified by faith — This is the sum of the preceding chapters. We have peace with God - Being enemies to God no longer, ver. 10; neither fearing his wrath, ver. 9. We have peace, hope, love, and power over sin, the sum of the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth chapters. These are the fruits of justifying faith: where these are not, that faith is not.
Into this grace — This state of favour.

We glory in tribulations also — Which we are so far from esteeming a mark of God's displeasure, that we receive them as tokens of his fatherly love, whereby we are prepared for a more exalted happiness. The Jews objected to the persecuted state of the Christians as inconsistent with the people of the Messiah. It is therefore with great propriety that the apostle so often mentions the blessings arising from this very thing.
And patience works more experience of the sincerity of our grace, and of God's power and faithfulness.

Hope shameth us not — That is, gives us the highest glorying. We glory in this our hope, because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts - The divine conviction of God's love to us, and that love to God which is both the earnest and the beginning of heaven. By the Holy Ghost - The efficient cause of all these present blessings, and the earnest of those to come.

How can we now doubt of God's love? For when we were without strength — Either to think, will, or do anything good. In due time - Neither too soon nor too late; but in that very point of time which the wisdom of God knew to be more proper than any other. Christ died for the ungodly - Not only to set them a pattern, or to procure them power to follow it. It does not appear that this expression, of dying for any one, has any other signification than that of rescuing the life of another by laying down our own.

A just man — One who gives to all what is strictly their due The good man - One who is eminently holy; full of love, of compassion, kindness, mildness, of every heavenly and amiable temper. Perhaps-one-would-even-dare to die - Every word increases the strangeness of the thing, and declares even this to be something great and unusual.

But God recommendeth — A most elegant expression. Those are wont to be recommended to us, who were before either unknown to, or alienated from, us. While we were sinners - So far from being good, that we were not even just.

By his blood — By his bloodshedding. We shall be saved from wrath through him - That is, from all the effects of the wrath of God. But is there then wrath in God? Is not wrath a human passion? And how can this human passion be in God? We may answer this by another question: Is not love a human passion? And how can this human passion be in God? But to answer directly: wrath in man, and so love in man, is a human passion. But wrath in God is not a human passion; nor is love, as it is in God. Therefore the inspired writers ascribe both the one and the other to God only in an analogical sense.

If — As sure as; so the word frequently signifies; particularly in this and the eighth chapter. We shalt be saved - Sanctified and glorified. Through his life - "Whoever liveth to make intercession for us."

And not only so, but we also glory — The whole sentence, from the third to the eleventh verse, may be taken together thus: We not only "rejoice in hope of the glory of God," but also in the midst of tribulations we glory in God himself through our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom we have now received the reconciliation.

glossa.text: *From faith.* Above he said, justified freely by grace, lest faith itself be proud. Let not the faithful man say: that I may merit justification, I have faith: for it is answered him: what hast thou that thou hast not received? *Let us have peace,* we who have been reconciled to him through Christ, the minister of grace.
*Through whom.* He enumerates the benefits that are had from Christ.

*Tribulation.* That tribulation does not take away patience, charity brings about, which is the proper gift of the Holy Spirit.

*Hope.* That is, the certitude of future glory, which to human reason seems empty: but it is confirmed by the testimony of virtue, that is, of patience or of miracles.

*But hope.* Because it is in God, who does not deceive, not in lying man; and the pledge of this hope is the Spirit: for it is read: *Let the fountain of thy water be thine own, and let no stranger have communication with thee ((Eccli. V))*; he himself is the Spirit, whom the wicked cannot receive, and he is charity, which no one can have and be wicked. But a man can have the name of Christ and baptism, receive the body of the Lord, and have the other sacraments, and be wicked. Charity therefore is the proper gift of the Spirit, and the singular fountain.

*The charity of God.* Or: God loves us widely: and we have this in our hearts through the Spirit, who makes us understand the charity of God toward us.

*For why.* Since God loves us, or we love him through the Spirit, hope will be fulfilled: because unless it be so, Christ suffered in vain. And this is why Christ [suffered] for the ungodly, that is, for love of the ungodly, or in their stead: for the ungodly, not those who had been so of old and were not so then, but when we were weak in sins.

*According to the time,* that is, for three days only, lest thou despair of the power of him whose good will appears in his death: from whom we receive such earnests, in that he gave to the ungodly his own death, who keeps for the just his own life. He died for thee, O mortal man, that thou mayest live with him. He took upon himself our death, that he might give us his own life: he received from thee that whereby he might die for thee. He clothed himself with that wherein he might die for thee: he will clothe thee with that wherein thou mayest live with him. He clothed himself with mortal flesh in the virginity of his mother: he will clothe thee with everlasting life in the equality of the Father.

*Scarcely.* He says, *for a just man.* Perhaps for a good man: he shows both to be difficult and rare, but the one more difficult and more rare.

*For a just man,* etc. A man is just by reason of his exercise, who is also good; but there is also a good man who is not just, that is, one who was born in simplicity: an innocent who has not yet laboured to enlarge himself with goods, such as are the little ones cleansed in baptism; and although the just man is the better, yet the cause of innocence is the more pitiable, rather than that of justice, because justice of this kind is not without severity.

*While yet.* Behold, while he hated us according to our sins, he loved us according to that which is his own work: which also he did before the constitution of the world. It had to be said how much he loved us, lest we should despair; and what manner of men we were, lest we should be proud. There was another way also possible to God, who can do all things, but none more fitting for the healing of our misery. For what so lifts us up, and frees us from despair of immortality, as that he made so much of us, that a man should die for us?

*Much more therefore.* It is a heavier thing to die for sin and to take away sin, than to save those already just and even co-operating. *In his blood.* Because thus the devil is overcome by justice, not by power. By justice, because the devil slew one undeserving, namely Christ: whence also he by right loses the others. Not by power, because the devil is a lover of power, a deserter of justice, wherein men imitate him the more. It pleased God therefore that, conquering not by power but by justice, he should rescue man, wherein man might imitate him: but afterwards, in the resurrection, power followed, because the dead man lived again, never afterwards to die.
*We were enemies.* Not sinners in any manner whatever. *We are reconciled.* Because before we were justly under the power of the devil, our nature being depraved by sin.

notes.text: Sychar — Formerly called Sichem or Shechem. Jacob gave - On his death bed, Gen. xlviii, 22.
Jesus sat down — Weary as he was. It was the sixth hour - Noon; the heat of the day.
Give me to drink — In this one conversation he brought her to that knowledge which the apostles were so long in attaining.
For his disciples were gone — Else he needed not have asked her.
How dost thou — Her open simplicity appears from her very first words. The Jews have no dealings - None by way of friendship. They would receive no kind of favour from them.

If thou hadst known the gift — The living water; and who it is - He who alone is able to give it: thou wouldst have asked of him - On those words the stress lies. Water - In like manner he draws the allegory from bread, chap. vi, 27, and from light, viii, 12; the first, the most simple, necessary, common, and salutary things in nature. Living water - The Spirit and its fruits. But she might the more easily mistake his meaning, because living water was a common phrase among the Jews for spring water.

Our father Jacob — So they fancied he was; whereas they were, in truth, a mixture of many nations, placed there by the king of Assyria, in the room of the Israelites whom he had carried away captive, 2 Kings xvii, 24. Who gave us the well - In Joseph their supposed forefather: and drank thereof - So even he had no better water than this.

Will never thirst — Will never (provided he continue to drink thereof) be miserable, dissatisfied, without refreshment. If ever that thirst returns, it will be the fault of the man, not the water. But the water that I shall give him - The spirit of faith working by love, shall become in him - An inward living principle, a fountain - Not barely a well, which is soon exhausted, springing up into everlasting life - Which is a confluence, or rather an ocean of streams arising from this fountain.
That I thirst not — She takes him still in a gross sense.
Jesus saith to her — He now clears the way that he might give her a better kind of water than she asked for. Go, call thy husband - He strikes directly at her bosom sin.
Thou hast well said — We may observe in all our Lord's discourses the utmost weightiness, and yet the utmost courtesy.
Thou hast had five husbands — Whether they were all dead or not, her own conscience now awakened would tell her.
Sir, I perceive — So soon was her heart touched.

The instant she perceived this, she proposes what she thought the most important of all questions. This mountain — Pointing to Mount Gerizim. Sanballat, by the permission of Alexander the Great, had built a temple upon Mount Gerizim, for Manasseh, who for marrying Sanballat's daughter had been expelled from the priesthood and from Jerusalem, Neh. xiii, 28. This was the place where the Samaritans used to worship in opposition to Jerusalem. And it was so near Sychar, that a man's voice might be heard from the one to the other. Our fathers worshipped - This plainly refers to Abraham and Jacob (from whom the Samaritans pretended to deduce their genealogy) who erected altars in this place: Gen. xii, 6, 7, and Gen. xxxiii, 18, 20. And possibly to the whole congregation, who were directed when they came into the land of Canaan to put the blessing upon Mount Gerizim, Deut. xi, 29. Ye Jews say, In Jerusalem is the place - Namely, the temple.

Believe me — Our Lord uses this expression in this manner but once; and that to a Samaritan. To his own people, the Jews, his usual language is, I say unto you. The hour cometh when ye - Both Samaritans and Jews, shall worship neither in this mountain, nor at Jerusalem - As preferable to any other place. True worship shall be no longer confined to any one place or nation.

Ye worship ye know not what — Ye Samaritans are ignorant, not only of the place, but of the very object of worship. Indeed, they feared the Lord after a fashion; but at the same time served their own gods, 2 Kings xvii, 33. Salvation is from the Jews - So spake all the prophets, that the saviour should arise out of the Jewish nation: and that from thence the knowledge of him should spread to all nations under heaven.
The true worshippers shall worship the Father — Not here or there only, but at all times and in all places.

God is a Spirit — Not only remote from the body, and all the properties of it, but likewise full of all spiritual perfections, power, wisdom, love, holiness. And our worship should be suitable to his nature. We should worship him with the truly spiritual worship of faith, love, and holiness, animating all our tempers, thoughts, words, and actions.
The woman saith — With joy for what she had already learned, and desire of fuller instruction.

Jesus saith — Hasting to satisfy her desire before his disciples came. l am He - Our Lord did not speak this so plainly to the Jews who were so full of the Messiah's temporal kingdom. If he had, many would doubtless have taken up arms in his favour, and others have accused him to the Roman governor. Yet he did in effect declare the thing, though he denied the particular title. For in a multitude of places he represented himself, both as the Son of man, and as the Son of God: both which expressions were generally understood by the Jews as peculiarly applicable to the Messiah.

His disciples marvelled that he talked with a woman — Which the Jewish rabbis reckoned scandalous for a man of distinction to do. They marvelled likewise at his talking with a woman of that nation, which was so peculiarly hateful to the Jews. Yet none said - To the woman, What seekest thou? - Or to Christ, Why talkest thou with her?
The woman left her water pot — Forgetting smaller things.

A man who told me all things that ever I did — Our Lord had told her but a few things. But his words awakened her conscience, which soon told her all the rest. Is not this the Christ? - She does not doubt of it herself, but incites them to make the inquiry.
In the meantime — Before the people came.
My meat — That which satisfies the strongest appetite of my soul.
The fields are white already — As if he had said, The spiritual harvest is ripe already. The Samaritans, ripe for the Gospel, covered the ground round about them.

He that reapeth — Whoever saves souls, receiveth wages - A peculiar blessing to himself, and gathereth fruit - Many souls: that he that soweth - Christ the great sower of the seed, and he that reapeth may rejoice together - In heaven.
That saying — A common proverb; One soweth - The prophets and Christ; another reapeth - The apostles and succeeding ministers.
I — he Lord of the whole harvest, have sent you - He had employed them already in baptizing, ver. 2.
We know that this is the saviour of the world — And not of the Jews only.

glossa.text:
*He cometh therefore.* That the Samaritans might acknowledge him and be converted to him, they who claimed for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch Israel.

*Which is called Sichar.* Sichar, that is, an enclosing, or a branch: that is, the Gentile people shut up under sin, which is a branch cut out of the wild olive and grafted into the olive.

*Now there was,* etc. Because natural reason rises from no other source than from the cause of all good things, therefore it is beautifully said to be the fount of Jacob, that is, the infinite reason proceeding from the height of the Father.

*Jesus therefore, being wearied,* etc. Allegorically. The journey of Jesus is the assumption of flesh, in which there is weariness, that is, infirmity, relieving the man whom his power created: the sitting is humility. The sixth hour, the sixth age in which he came; the well, the depth of this world. The Samaritan woman is the Church, coming not now just, but to be justified. The water of the well is the will of this world, which is drawn as it were out of the deep by men let down and bent toward it, with covetousness sent before like a water-pot. *He was sitting.* As one relieving weariness, wherein is indicated the master who is to teach those who draw near and to possess them. *Upon.* It is called a fount wherever water flows from the earth; but if at the surface, a fount only; if in the deep, it is also called a well.

*There cometh.* In the figure of the Church of the Gentiles, which formerly drew water, that is, the pleasure of the deep of the world; whose faith Jesus thirsts for, and asks to be given drink by her.

((GREG.)) Or the woman, that is, the Synagogue, who came to draw water, etc., *as far as* the primitive Church.

*Give me.* Jesus, sitting upon the fount, asks of the primitive Church, which he had chosen out of the Gentiles, the drink of faith by which men believe in him; he asks of nature the drink of reason by which the Creator and Redeemer is searched out. The apostles are sent into the city, that is, into the world, to buy spiritual foods, that is, faith and action and knowledge, with which the teachers of the Church are filled. *Give me.* Although Jesus could thirst after his weariness, yet he does not demand this drink, but he desires that the heart of the Church of the Gentiles should be made a draught for him in acknowledgement of his labour.

*For the disciples.* The disciples went away into the city, namely to the Jews, who are fenced by the valley of the law and armed with the darts of prophecy, that they might buy their foods, namely preparing their hearts for God by the preaching of the faith.

*She saith therefore.* Not knowing what drink he asks of her, and thinking that it was of the water, she objects that she is of the vessels of strangers, whose company also the Jews do not use; but Jesus, who was asking for faith, desired to give her the Spirit, and admonishes her to ask; and the Spirit is both the gift of God and living water.

*For not,* etc. The Jews execrate the Samaritans and call them supplanters, because they deprived them of the inheritance of their father Jacob by abstaining from their foods and their vessels.
*Jesus answered.* Step by step and in simple words he instructs her, that at length she may be able to receive the gift of God, that is, the Spirit.

*The woman said to him.* That is called living water, and no other, save that which is caught where it rises; of which the woman, savouring carnally, said: Since thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep, how hast thou living water? But lest perchance he should seem to promise another fount, she adds: Art thou better, that is, canst thou be better than Jacob, who used this one with his own? Against which therefore Christ openly shows that he speaks not carnally but spiritually, saying that he shall not thirst who has drunk his water.

*Art thou.* Being a stranger, she calls Jacob her father, because she herself had lived under the law of Moses, and possessed the field which Jacob had given to his son.

((AUG.)) The little vessel is covetousness, the water is pleasure; it is refreshed, not extinguished.

 *And he himself drank thereof.* Men and cattle drink of the well, and likewise of reason: as though depraved and darkened, it is dug out and worked with great labour. But some drink as men, who use that reason for good, as the saints; some as cattle, who use it for evil, as the philosophers.

*But he that.* Whosoever shall lend his heart to my preaching and shall acknowledge the gift of grace, the faith which works through love is born in him, and so at length he shall pass over into life eternal.
*Water.* Bodily water flows downward; spiritual water leaps upward, and carries up with itself into eternal glory those who drink it.

*Go, call thy husband,* etc. That under his leading thou mayest ascend to the contemplation of spiritual understanding: *go, call thy husband.* Thou who art sensual, call the rational understanding, that thou mayest be governed by it as by a husband; thou who now savourest carnally, him will I, the light and head of the man, enlighten. As if he should say: These things which I say are to be understood not carnally, as thou, being animal, dost, but spiritually, and are to be received under the leading of reason; and therefore do thou prepare thy understanding for me and come, by understanding these spiritual things which I say.

*The woman answered.* In truth this woman then had no husband, but was making use of a certain man not lawful, of whom she answers, still savouring carnally, she who had not yet called her husband, that is, her understanding. *Jesus saith to her.* Raising her little by little, he speaks still in mysteries, that little by little he might bring her to know who it was that spoke with her. And he praises not the good work, nor the prudent answer of the woman, but he praises the confession of the truth.

*For thou hast had five husbands.* The five husbands are the five laws given to human nature. The first, in paradise before sin, in the prohibition of the tree. The second, after the transgression and the expulsion from paradise, concerning the multiplication of the human stock. The third, to Noah before the flood, concerning the building of the ark. The fourth, after the flood, concerning the divisions of the nations. The fifth, to Abraham, concerning circumcision and the immolation of his son. To these five laws, as to five husbands, the human soul was subject from the beginning of the world until Moses: afterward the law of the letter was given, which conferred no salvation; whence it is said: *He whom thou now hast is not thy husband.* Put away the letter; go to the spirit of the letter, to the New Testament, from which thou mayest conceive a spiritual offspring of virtues.

((AUG.)) The five husbands, that is, the five senses of the body, ruled thee; now, in the time of discretion, a husband, that is, the understanding of wisdom, does not rule thee, but an adulterer, that is, error, corrupts thee, while thou receivest carnally the things I say; and therefore call thy husband, that (as I say) thou mayest understand spiritually. Therefore the five senses in the lesser age are called husbands, because they are lawful. For after the fall of man, and by the decree of God, that age is naturally governed, not toward eternal things, but toward the seeking of these temporal things if they soothe, and the shunning of them if they offend.

*That thou art a prophet.* The woman, profiting from what she had heard, had already begun to have understanding in some measure, whence she also calls him a prophet; but not full understanding, because she does not believe that Christ has come.

*Our loaves,* etc. Thou art a prophet, and therefore judge concerning this contention which moves me. The Jews set themselves before the Samaritans on account of the temple which Solomon built, in which they worshipped. On the contrary the Samaritans set themselves against the Jews on account of the mountain, on which, and not in the temple, the fathers worshipped who pleased God. And so the patriarchs worshipped on the mountains, the Jews in the temple, prefiguring the manner of praying well.

*Woman.* In this place the Lord represses the boasting of the Samaritans, who thought that they had been of no less religion than the Jews. He speaks therefore in the person of the prophets and of all who believe in Christ; whence he says: *You adore the Father whom you know not,* because no one adores the Father unless he adore the Son, through whom one comes to the knowledge of the Father; but we know the Son, and through the Son the Father; whence follows: *For salvation is of the Jews,* etc., that is, because Christ, who is salvation, is of the Jews, not only by the origin of the flesh, but from them also arose the faith and the primitive Church. *Believe me.* Because there is already in thee a husband who can believe, and therefore to believe: *For unless thou shalt have believed, thou shalt not understand ((Isa.))* . *When neither on the mountain.* Behold, your mountain and the temple of the Jews shall alike be reprobated; but in this you are unequal, that you Samaritans adore what you know not, but we Jews, not all, but the elect, adore what we know, because to us is the knowledge of God, the testament, the promised prophecy: of us is Christ; and this is, *for salvation is of the Jews,* but although we are thus different, yet I do not prefer the place of the Jews to the place of the Samaritans, and this is.

*But the hour cometh, and now is, when.* Before I came in the flesh, no one could adore the Father in spirit and in truth, except the patriarchs and the prophets, to whom my incarnation had been revealed; but through my presence in the flesh there shall be true adorers.

*In spirit and in truth.* Not in the temple, not on this mountain, but inwardly, in the innermost temple of the heart, and in the truth of knowledge, is the Father to be adored.

*God is a spirit.* Since God is a spirit and not a body, he does not seek a bodily place, a mountain or a temple, in which he may be prayed to; but a pure spirit is his temple, in which he is to be prayed to, not concerning visible things which pass away, but concerning the eternal things which are truth.

*I know that the Messias cometh, who is called,* etc. Now advanced further by the words of him who taught her, she knows by whom she ought to be perfectly instructed, that is, by the Messias. *He will tell us all things. Jesus saith to her.* He will show in what manner, the temple and the mountain being despised, we may adore in spirit and in truth, and how, the shadows being cast away, we may be illumined by the truth. *I am he that speak.* Him whom thou awaitest as one to come, know that he has come; and, having brought with thee the husband who is to govern thee, labour to learn the things that are necessary to faith. And because she already knew who could teach her, although she did not recognize him who was already teaching her, she was worthy that he should manifest himself to her; whence he says: *I am the Messias,* which manifestation once received, she has nothing further to seek; whence follows: *She left therefore her water-pot,* etc. But the Evangelist interposes somewhat concerning the disciples.

*And they wondered that.* They did not wonder that he was speaking with a woman, with such as he had been accustomed to speak with, but that it was with a stranger, being ignorant of the mystery of the Church that was to be of the Gentiles. And they suspect no evil, but wonder at his clemency, because he teaches a Gentile woman in error, as *he who came to seek that which had perished.*

*She left therefore.* Having heard *I am he,* the woman, now holding Christ in her understanding as the head of the man, left the water-pot, that is, covetousness, and ran to preach the gospel. Here let those who are to preach the gospel learn first to lay aside the care and the burden of this world.
*Come and see.* Step by step she leads those rude ones to the truth; nor does she at once affirm him to be Christ, lest they should be angered and take offence.
*Hath any man brought.* They did not dare to question the Lord, fearing lest they should be reproved by him if they questioned incautiously.

*My meat is.* They did not understand the food, just as the woman above did not understand the water; whence the master instructs them, not by a circuit as he did her, but now openly, saying: *My meat is to do,* etc. *His will.* The Father's. The will of the Father is that men believe in him, that is, in the Son whom he himself sent. The work of the Father is our salvation. Christ's meat, therefore, is our faith and our salvation. He does the will, then, by teaching men to believe in him; he does the work by bringing the mystery of redemption to maturity.

*Do you not say.* Since he seeks the faith and the salvation of the peoples, he grows fervent for the work and disposes to send labourers. *Lift up your eyes.* Consider with the understanding of the mind that, the winter being past, that is, unbelief, the warmth of faith is at hand and hearts are made ready, that you may gather from them the works of justice; as if he should say: Help toward the fulfilling of the Father's will. And well can you do it, because the harvest is ready, that is, see the Gentiles believing easily.

*That both he that soweth.* Both were needed, the sower and the reaper, because in this the word appears probable, that one sows and another reaps; for unless they had been made ready through the prophets, they would not have heard the apostles.

*I have sent you.* I make you reapers there where others have sown, that is, in Judaea, where the first crop was gathered, whence some going forth have sown in the whole world, whence another harvest rises as it were from the grains, to be gathered at the end of the world by the angels as reapers. *They have laboured, and you have entered into their labours.* For many were the labours of the patriarchs and the prophets, in all of which was the prophecy of Christ, and they suffered many things as it were in the cold of the sowing.

*When they were come.* First they heard the report, afterward they beheld him present; and it is not enough for them, but they make him abide with them, that they may be instructed by his own words, which they prefer to the words of the woman. In all which, on the contrary, the hardness of the Jews is reproved, who do not believe even at miracles. *And he abode there two.* Morally. So daily among those who are without, Christ is announced through the woman, that is, the Church, and they believe through that report. Thence he abides with them for two days without mention of night, that their light may be instructed by the two precepts of charity.

*And they said to the woman.* After the Lord, by the presence of the flesh, the Jews being spiritually taught, had poured the grace of his own knowledge into the woman, that is, into the law, they said: now not on account of thy speech do we believe.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: "Justified by faith" (5:1) is the conclusion Paul has just drawn from Abraham (Romans 4), and ultimately rests on Genesis 15:6, "Abram believed the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." The faith-righteousness link governing 5:1 is verbally and conceptually the Genesis 15:6 logic carried forward into this pericope's opening clause.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
echoes.note: "Peace with God" (5:1) and reconciliation through Christ's death (5:10-11) echo the Suffering Servant whose "chastisement brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed." Isaiah 53 supplies the template of one man's death securing peace and healing for the many that drives the whole passage.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: "While we were yet sinners/ungodly" Christ died for us (5:6, 5:8): "All we like sheep have gone astray... and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all." The Servant bearing the iniquity of the straying matches Paul's "Christ died for the ungodly."

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: "God's love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit" (5:5): "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh." The verb "pour out" (ekcheo) applied to the Spirit is the prophetic eschatological-outpouring idiom; Paul quotes Joel 2:32 at Romans 10:13, showing the passage is in view.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: "The righteous shall live by faith" is Paul's thesis text (Romans 1:17) and stands behind "being justified by faith" (5:1). The faith-life pairing of Habakkuk 2:4 resonates in the move from justification by faith to being "saved by his life" (5:10), though no verbal quotation appears here.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: "He poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many" stands behind "Christ died for us" while sinners (5:8) and "justified by his blood" (5:9). The Servant's vicarious death for "many" anticipates the many/one structure Paul develops.

echoes.text: For the life of the flesh is in the blood; and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life.
echoes.note: "Justified by his blood" (5:9): "the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement." Paul's atoning-blood language draws on the Levitical principle that blood effects expiation, already invoked at Romans 3:25 (hilasterion).

echoes.text: But let all those who take refuge in you rejoice, Let them always shout for joy, because you defend them. Let them also who love your name be joyful in you.
echoes.note: "We rejoice in hope of the glory of God" and "rejoice in God" (5:2, 5:11): "let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy... let those who love your name exult in you." The pattern of those justified/sheltered by God rejoicing/exulting in him is a recurrent Psalmic posture Paul takes up.

echoes.text: They cried to you, and were delivered. They trusted in you, and were not disappointed.
echoes.note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "they trusted in you and were not put to shame." The Psalmic confession that trust in God does not end in shame is the verbal-conceptual root of Paul's claim that hope ou kataischynei.

echoes.text: Yes, no one who waits for you shall be shamed. They shall be shamed who deal treacherously without cause.
echoes.note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "none who wait for you shall be put to shame." Psalm 25 (vv. 3, 20) repeatedly grounds the assurance that hope in God is not disappointed, matching Paul's claim about hope.

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: "Hope does not put us to shame" (5:5): "whoever believes will not be put to shame" (LXX). Paul quotes this very verse at Romans 9:33 and 10:11; the same shame/faith formula colors his statement here that hope does not disappoint.

echoes.text: For I will pour water on him who is thirsty, and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit on your seed, and my blessing on your offspring:
echoes.note: "God's love poured out... through the Holy Spirit" (5:5): "I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring." The same Spirit-outpouring promise, paired with water/blessing imagery, undergirds Paul's image of love flooding the heart by the Spirit.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: "Poured out into our hearts... the Holy Spirit who was given to us" (5:5): "I will give you a new heart... I will put my Spirit within you." The new-covenant promise of God's Spirit placed within the heart matches Paul's interiorized gift of the Spirit and love.

echoes.text: My son, if you come to serve the Lord, Prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, And make not haste in time of calamity. Cleave to him, and depart not, That you may be increased at your latter end. Accept whatever is brought upon you, And be longsuffering when you passest into humiliation. For gold is tried in the fire, And acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation.
echoes.note: "Suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance proven character" (5:3-4): "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare yourself for testing... for gold is tested in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation." A Second Temple wisdom commonplace that trials refine and prove the faithful, closely parallel to Paul's chain suffering->endurance->proven character.

echoes.text: And having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; Because God made trial of them, and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, And as a whole burnt offering he accepted them.
echoes.note: "Suffering works perseverance... proven character; and proven character, hope" (5:3-4): "Having been disciplined a little, they will receive great good, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself; like gold in the furnace he tried them." Second Temple parallel linking testing/discipline to being proven worthy and to hope of glory (cf. Wisdom 3:4, hope full of immortality).

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: "Justified by his blood" (5:9) may faintly recall the blood of the covenant Moses dashed on the people, sealing the relationship with God. Disputed as a deliberate echo here versus general sacrificial background.

echoes.text: The work of righteousness will be peace; and the effect of righteousness, quietness and confidence forever.
echoes.note: "Peace with God" through righteousness (5:1): "the work of righteousness shall be peace." The prophetic linkage of righteousness and peace faintly underlies Paul's pairing of justification with peace, though no verbal borrowing is evident.

echoes.text: I will hear what God, Yahweh, will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, his saints; but let them not turn again to folly. Surely his salvation is near those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land. Mercy and truth meet together. Righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
echoes.note: "Peace with God" (5:1): "righteousness and peace kiss each other." The Psalm's union of righteousness and peace as God's salvific gift resonates faintly with Paul's justification-yields-peace claim. Disputed as a deliberate echo.

echoes.text: I create the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says Yahweh; “and I will heal them.”
echoes.note: "Peace with God" for the reconciled (5:1, 5:10-11): "Peace, peace, to the far and the near, says the LORD; and I will heal him." The prophetic announcement of peace and healing to estranged people faintly anticipates peace and reconciliation language. Contested.

echoes.text: Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram; and encamped before the city. He bought the parcel of ground where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for one hundred pieces of money.
echoes.note: Sychar lies near the plot of ground at Shechem that Jacob purchased; v5's 'parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph' anchors the scene in this patriarchal land-grant. High Volume (named geography) and Coherence with John's Jacob/Joseph framing.

echoes.text: Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”
echoes.note: Jacob's deathbed gift of an extra 'portion' (shekem/Shechem) to Joseph is the explicit referent of v5, where the well stands on land Jacob gave Joseph. Strong verbal-thematic Coherence; the giving-of-portion motif underwrites the woman's later 'our father Jacob who gave us the well.'

echoes.text: Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east. He looked, and behold, a well in the field, and, behold, three flocks of sheep lying there by it. For out of that well they watered the flocks. The stone on the well’s mouth was large. There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone again on the well’s mouth in its place. Jacob said to them, “My […]
echoes.note: The classic betrothal type-scene: a man journeys, sits/stops at a well, a woman comes to draw, water is given, she runs to tell her household. v6 'sat down by the well' mirrors Jacob meeting Rachel at the well. High Recurrence (three OT instances) and Volume; the reader primed for betrothal finds a startling inversion.

echoes.text: The servant took ten camels, of his master’s camels, and departed, having a variety of good things of his master’s with him. He arose, and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor. He made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time that women go out to draw water. He said, “Yahweh, the God of my master Abraham, please give me success this day, and show kindness to my master Abraham. Behold, I am standing […]
echoes.note: The Rebekah betrothal scene at the well: servant asks 'give me a drink,' woman draws, kinship and marriage follow. John's scene reuses the well-meeting template down to the request for water (v7). Strong Volume and Recurrence; coheres with the type-scene channel John exploits.

echoes.text: They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem, in the parcel of ground which Jacob bought of the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. They became the inheritance of the children of Joseph.
echoes.note: Joseph's bones were buried in the parcel at Shechem that Jacob bought, the same patriarchal plot John names. Availability and Coherence are strong; it reinforces the Jacob-Joseph-Shechem matrix even if John cites no text.

echoes.text: Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock. The shepherds came and drove them away; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock. When they came to Reuel, their father, he said, “How is it that you […]
echoes.note: Moses, a stranger in foreign territory (Midian), sits by a well where women come to draw; betrothal to Zipporah follows. As the third betrothal-at-well scene it raises Recurrence, strengthening the type even if the verbal contact with John is looser than Genesis 24/29.

echoes.text: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
echoes.note: Israel forsook the LORD, 'the fountain of living waters,' for broken cisterns; Jesus offers the 'living water' (hydor zon) the woman cannot draw from a deep well. High Volume (rare exact phrase 'living water/fountain of living waters') and Coherence: Jesus is the true fountain over against a cistern that cannot hold.

echoes.text: Yahweh, the hope of Israel, all who forsake you shall be disappointed. Those who depart from me shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken Yahweh, the spring of living waters.
echoes.note: Those who forsake the LORD have forsaken 'the fountain of living waters'; the doubled Jeremianic phrase raises Recurrence and makes the divine self-identification as living-water source the most likely source-pool for v10-14.

echoes.text: The servant ran to meet her, and said, “Please give me a drink, a little water from your pitcher.”
echoes.note: Eliezer's 'Let me drink, I pray thee' to Rebekah at the well is verbally echoed by Jesus' 'Give me a drink' (v7), continuing the betrothal type-scene into the dialogue itself. Volume is moderate (short shared phrase) but Coherence with the well-meeting frame is high.

echoes.text: It will happen in that day, that living waters will go out from Jerusalem; half of them toward the eastern sea, and half of them toward the western sea; in summer and in winter will it be.
echoes.note: On the eschatological day 'living waters shall go out from Jerusalem.' Jesus relocates that eschatological living water into himself given to a Samaritan, fitting John's realized-eschatology and the 'hour comes and now is' just ahead. Moderate Volume, strong thematic Coherence.

echoes.text: Therefore with joy you will draw water out of the wells of salvation.
echoes.note: 'With joy shall you draw water out of the wells of salvation' joins drawing water (the woman's task) to salvation (v22 'salvation is from the Jews'). Coherence is good; the drawing-water verb links the literal and figural planes.

echoes.text: “Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat! Yes, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
echoes.note: 'Everyone who thirsts, come to the waters... without money' parallels Jesus' free 'gift of God' (v10) of water that ends thirst (v14). Strong Coherence with John's thirst/gift language; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: and Yahweh will guide you continually, and satisfy your soul in dry places, and make strong your bones; and you shall be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters don’t fail.
echoes.note: The blessed will be 'like a spring of water, whose waters fail not' — the interior, never-failing spring matches v14's 'well of water springing up to eternal life.' Coherence high on the perpetual-inner-spring image; Volume modest.

echoes.text: He brought me back to the door of the house; and behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward; (for the forefront of the house was toward the east;) and the waters came down from under, from the right side of the house, on the south of the altar. Then he brought me out by the way of the gate northward, and led me round by the way outside to the outer gate, by the way of the gate that looks toward the east; and behold, there ran […]
echoes.note: The life-giving river flowing from the temple, deepening and bringing life, is a leading source for NT living-water imagery. John makes Jesus the temple-source of the eschatological water; moderate Volume, strong Coherence with the temple/water/life nexus.

echoes.text: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.
echoes.note: 'With you is the fountain of life' grounds the divine-fountain motif; Jesus' gift becomes 'a well of water springing up to eternal life' (v14). Coherence with the life-fountain image is high; Volume modest.

echoes.text: They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'those who drink me will thirst for more'; Jesus inverts it — whoever drinks his water 'will never thirst again' (v14). Likely deliberate contrast with the sapiential tradition; Availability secure as Second-Temple deuterocanon.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: The redeemed 'shall not hunger nor thirst,' for God leads them by springs of water — paralleling 'never thirst again' (v14). Faint, but coherent with the never-thirst promise.

echoes.text: The words of a man’s mouth are like deep waters. The fountain of wisdom is like a flowing brook.
echoes.note: 'The wellspring of wisdom is a flowing brook' and Proverbs' fountain-of-life sayings supply the sapiential backdrop for water = life/wisdom. Faint verbal contact; contributes to the broader well/fountain field.

echoes.text: a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing streams from Lebanon. Beloved
echoes.note: The beloved is 'a well of living waters' — a rare exact match to 'living water,' and, given the betrothal type-scene already in play, a thematically apt nuptial overtone. Volume on the phrase is notable but the connection is contested.

echoes.text: Isaac’s servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of springing water.
echoes.note: Isaac's servants find 'a well of springing water' (be'er mayim chayyim) — the same idiom rendered 'well of water springing up' in v14, set again in patriarchal well-digging. Reinforces the patriarchal-well + living-water overlap.

echoes.text: The king of Assyria brought men from Babylon, and from Cuthah, and from Avva, and from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the children of Israel; and they possessed Samaria, and lived in the cities of it. So it was, at the beginning of their dwelling there, that they didn’t fear Yahweh: therefore Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them. Therefore they spoke to the king of Assyria, saying, “The […]
echoes.note: The Samaritans were resettled foreign peoples who 'feared the LORD and served their own gods'; the woman's 'five husbands' has long been read as a figure for this syncretism (Josephus counts five settler nations/deities). Coherence with John's Samaritan setting is high, though the allegory of the number is debated.

echoes.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts; Lest I strip her naked, and make her bare as in the day that she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and set her like a dry land, and kill her with thirst. Indeed, on her children I will have no mercy; for they are children of unfaithfulness; For their mother has played […]
echoes.note: Israel as the adulterous wife pursuing many lovers/baalim supplies the prophetic marriage-and-apostasy grammar behind the husbands motif. Faint and contested, but coherent with reading the woman's marital history as covenantal figure.

echoes.text: (In earlier times in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, thus he said, “Come, and let us go to the seer”; for he who is now called a prophet was before called a Seer.)
echoes.note: The prophet as 'seer' who knows hidden things lies behind the woman's 'I perceive you are a prophet' (v19) after Jesus discloses her secret. Faint lexical contact; supports the prophet-recognition motif.

echoes.text: It shall happen, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land where you go to possess it, that you shall set the blessing on Mount Gerizim, and the curse on Mount Ebal.
echoes.note: The blessing was set on Mount Gerizim, the Samaritan holy mountain the woman means by 'this mountain' (v20). High Volume and Availability: the Gerizim/Jerusalem dispute is the precise OT fault-line John dramatizes.

echoes.text: But to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, you shall seek his habitation, and there you shall come. There you shall bring your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the wave offering of your hand, your vows, your freewill offerings, and the firstborn of your herd and of your flock. There you shall eat before Yahweh your God, and you shall rejoice in all that you put your hand to, you and […]
echoes.note: Worship is to be at 'the place the LORD shall choose,' the Deuteronomic charter behind the Jewish claim that 'in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship' (v20). High Coherence: Jesus transcends the very 'place' debate this text founds (v21-23).

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: Moses promised a prophet 'like me' who would speak all God commands; the Samaritan Taheb expectation rests here, matching the woman's 'when Messiah comes he will declare to us all things' (v25). High Coherence with Samaritan messianism and Jesus' 'I am he' (v26).

echoes.text: “These shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people, when you have passed over the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.
echoes.note: Six tribes stand on Gerizim to pronounce blessing, grounding the Samaritan claim that 'our fathers worshiped in this mountain.' Coheres with v20; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Therefore my people shall know my name. Therefore they shall know in that day that I am he who speaks; behold, it is I.”
echoes.note: 'My people shall know my name... that I am he that speaks' supplies the divine 'I am he' (ego eimi ho lalon) Jesus uses in v26, knitting revelation-of-name to direct speech. Volume is strong on the unusual 'he that speaks / I am he' formula.

echoes.text: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: Nations stream to Zion, for 'out of Zion shall go forth the law' — backing 'salvation is from the Jews' (v22). Coherence good for the Jew-as-source-of-salvation claim; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM,” and he said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
echoes.note: The divine self-naming 'I AM' stands behind John's recurring ego eimi, here in v26. Faint at this point (the absolute uses come later in John), but Availability and Coherence with John's theme are real.

echoes.text: Now the Egyptians are men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When Yahweh stretches out his hand, both he who helps shall stumble, and he who is helped shall fall, and they all shall be consumed together.
echoes.note: 'The Egyptians are flesh, and not spirit' gives the flesh/spirit contrast informing 'God is spirit' (v24). Faint and contested, but a plausible OT seed for the spirit-worship claim.

echoes.text: The young lady ran, and told her mother’s house about these words.
echoes.note: Rebekah 'ran and told' her household after the well encounter; the woman leaves her water pot and runs to tell the city (v28-29), completing the betrothal type-scene's go-and-announce beat. Faint verbal contact but coherent with the type-scene already established.

echoes.text: “Behold, the days come,” says Yahweh, “that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the one treading grapes him who sows seed; and sweet wine will drip from the mountains, and flow from the hills.
echoes.note: The eschatological harvest where 'the plowman overtakes the reaper' — sowing and reaping collapse together — underlies 'fields white for harvest already' and sower-and-reaper rejoicing together (v35-36). High Coherence with realized harvest; Volume strong on the compressed-harvest image.

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: Man lives not by bread alone but by what proceeds from God's mouth; Jesus' 'I have food you don't know about... to do the will of him who sent me' (v32-34) reuses this contrast of bodily food with God's word/will. Strong Coherence; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe' supplies the ripe/ready harvest call behind v35. Coherence is good, though Joel's harvest is judgment, making the transfer to mission-harvest somewhat contested.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: Those who sow in tears reap in joy, going out and returning rejoicing — matching 'he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together' (v36). Coherence good on the joint sow/reap rejoicing; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: I haven’t gone back from the commandment of his lips. I have treasured up the words of his mouth more than my necessary food.
echoes.note: 'I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food' parallels Jesus' food-as-doing-God's-will. Faint, supporting the word/will-over-food motif.

echoes.text: You will sow, but won’t reap. You will tread the olives, but won’t anoint yourself with oil; and crush grapes, but won’t drink the wine.
echoes.note: 'You shall sow but not reap' typifies the sow-one/reap-another proverb cited in v37. One of several covenant-curse/proverb backgrounds; faint individually.

echoes.text: then let me sow, and let another eat. Yes, let the produce of my field be rooted out.
echoes.note: 'Let me sow, and another eat' is a close formal analogue to the proverb 'one sows and another reaps' (v37). Faint but apt for the sowing/reaping-by-different-parties saying.

echoes.text: yes, he says, “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give you for a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”
echoes.note: The Servant made 'salvation to the ends of the earth' / light to the nations stands behind 'the Savior of the world' confessed by Samaritans (v42), extending salvation beyond Israel. Strong Coherence with the universal-salvation theme; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: 'A just God and a Savior... look unto me, all the ends of the earth' is the OT locus for God as universal Savior, reframed as 'Savior of the world.' Volume good on the Savior-for-all-earth formula.

echoes.text: Yahweh has made bare his holy arm in the eyes of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
echoes.note: 'All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God' supports the world-wide Savior confession in v42. Faint but coherent with the universalizing of salvation.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us' may color the deliberate 'he stayed there two days' (v40) before life/belief spreads, given John's symbolic use of time. Faint and contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The way is long, and we are thirsty.
We seek the living water of Jesus.
You met a stranger at the well at noon.
Give us this water, that we never thirst again.
You struck the rock in the desert, and the people drank.
Come, let us worship; let us not harden our hearts.
Come to the spring that rises to eternal life.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Noon, and the heat presses down; you stop at the well, dusty and thirsty, with no bucket and a long way still to go.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
A stranger is sitting there, and he asks you for a drink, and somehow he knows everything you have ever done.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
He offers water you cannot draw from any well, a spring that rises up inside you to eternal life.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Long ago he split the rock in the wilderness and the desert ran with streams; he has not run dry.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So come, all who are thirsty; come and drink. Come, let us worship and not harden our hearts.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Give us this water. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The road is dry; we come to the well thirsty.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You give the water that becomes a spring within us.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You struck the rock, and the desert ran with streams.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Come, let us drink; come, let us worship.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
